acts.head: Keep a paint oven hot all day and every car pays for it.
acts.sub: At this car plant the paint shop uses 44% of production energy. Energy is nearly 12% of what it costs to build a car.

acts.head: Simple rules switch off too late.
acts.sub: A threshold rule watches the queue. To avoid delays it keeps the oven hot, and saves only 15% against always-on.

acts.head: See the cars coming, then schedule the oven.
acts.sub: Live car positions feed a digital twin that predicts arrivals. The oven drops to standby or off in the gaps: 41% less energy per car than the threshold rule.

acts.head: How far ahead does the plant need to see?
acts.sub: Cost falls as visibility grows, most between 40 and 70 cars ahead. Past that, extra foresight adds little.

endTitle: See it coming, switch it off
endTag: Cars waited 35% longer, about three minutes each, for 41% less oven energy.

post.linkedin:
Knowing when the next car will arrive cut a paint oven's energy per car by 41% in a new study. No new oven, just a better schedule.

New open-access research in the International Journal of Production Research, from authors at the University of Mannheim, Özyeğin University and others, looks at a special-colour paint oven serving about 100 cars a day. At this plant the paint shop uses 44% of production energy.

Keeping it always on uses the equivalent of 10.1 minutes of full heat per car. A threshold rule that watches the queue only gets that to 8.6, because it keeps the oven hot to avoid delays. Feed live car positions into a digital twin, predict arrivals, and schedule the oven into standby or off in the gaps: 5.1 minutes per car, 41% less than the threshold rule.

The price is waiting. Cars waited about 35% longer, roughly three minutes each instead of just over two. And the plant doesn't need perfect foresight: the biggest gains came as visibility grew from 40 to 70 cars ahead, with smaller gains beyond that.

Which energy-heavy asset in your plant still runs on "keep it hot just in case"?
